meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I sincerely believe that banking institutions are more dangerous to our liberties than standing armies'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Jefferson in substance, but misquoted: he wrote “banking establishments… more dangerous than standing armies” in an 1816 letter to John Taylor.

answer.label: Thomas Jefferson — but a slight misquotation of his real words
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment is genuinely Jefferson’s, from his letter to John Taylor of 28 May 1816 — but he wrote “banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies,” not “banking institutions … more dangerous to our liberties than standing armies.” The popular wording swaps a word and inserts “to our liberties,” and it is often padded out with a wholly fabricated passage about private banks, “inflation” and “deflation.”

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: “banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies”
Slight misquotation of a genuine line

source.excerpt: And I sincerely believe, with you, that banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies; and that the principle of spending money to be paid by posterity, under the name of funding, is but swindling futurity on a large scale.
trail: The genuine line appears in Jefferson’s 28 May 1816 letter to John Taylor, transcribed by the National Archives.
The full letter text confirms he wrote “banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies” — not “institutions” or “to our liberties.”
Monticello’s Jefferson scholars label the popular wording a misquotation and the longer “inflation/deflation” expansion spurious.
source.excerptNote: Jefferson’s actual sentence in the 1816 letter to John Taylor. The popular quote replaces “establishments” with “institutions,” drops “with you,” and inserts “to our liberties.”

source.rightsNote: The genuine sentence comes from Jefferson’s 28 May 1816 letter to John Taylor, published long ago and firmly in the public domain (Jefferson died in 1826). The popular misquotation is only a two-word alteration of that public-domain text and creates no new rights; the padded “inflation/deflation” expansion has no identifiable authored source.

author.heading: About Thomas Jefferson
author.bio: Thomas Jefferson was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence and the third President of the United States. A lifelong opponent of concentrated financial power, he corresponded extensively on banking, public debt, and the dangers he believed a national banking system posed to a republic of independent citizens.

misattribution.heading: What’s really going on
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual: the attribution to Jefferson is essentially correct, but the exact wording that circulates is a slight misquotation — and it is frequently bolted onto a passage Jefferson never wrote at all.

items.why: Jefferson’s real sentence reads “banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies” — not “banking institutions … more dangerous to our liberties than standing armies.” The word “institutions” and the phrase “to our liberties” were introduced later, per Monticello.

The extended chain-email version — “If the American people ever allow private banks to control the issue of their currency, first by inflation, then by deflation…” — appears nowhere in Jefferson’s writings; the terms “inflation” and “deflation” were not used in this economic sense until after his death, and the passage is documented as spurious by Monticello.

misattribution.truthLine: Jefferson genuinely wrote that “banking establishments are more dangerous than standing armies” in his 28 May 1816 letter to John Taylor — the popular wording is a slight paraphrase, and the “private banks / inflation / deflation” expansion is a later fabrication.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Jefferson wrote to the Virginia statesman John Taylor of Caroline in 1816, responding to Taylor’s book attacking the banking and funding systems. Jefferson agreed emphatically, calling banking a “blot” on the constitutions and denouncing public debt passed to future generations as “swindling futurity on a large scale.”

His comparison of banks to standing armies — the era’s classic symbol of a threat to republican liberty — is why the line resonates today, and why it is so often pressed into service in modern debates over central banking and the Federal Reserve, usually in its altered form.
